title: Verify the Claim: Rise of poverty rates in Philadelphia Neighbourhoods
text:
Part 1 — Reconstruct
The WHYY article claims that poverty has risen from 2006-10 to 2013-17 based on the ACS five-year estimate. They have also quoted several neighbourhoods and calculated corresponding figures to prove their claim.
To verify their claims, I will be pulling the exact data from tidycensus to reconstruct (hopefully) similar figures and verify their statistical validity:

Years and survey: ACS5 for 2010 and 2017

The two periods do not overlap as there is a gap between 2010 (the end of the first survey) and 2013 (the start of the second survey). This will avoid error generated from comparing the same information twice and does not display the full change in characteristic between the 2 years.

Variable code: B07012_001, B07012_002

Based on the article that mentions “poverty rate” with margins of error, we need to compute poverty rate from the number of people below the poverty line (_002) divided by total population (_001).

Level: Tract

To roughly equate tracts to neighbourhoods that were compared in the article


Assumptions: For simplistic reasons, I assume 1 tract will correspond to 1 neighbourhood referred to in the article. The corresponding tract number is found by inputting a random address in a residential area of the referenced neighbourhood into the Census Geocoder.


1a. Pulling data
Pulling data from the census, we manipulate the data to get a wide dataframe with columns:

GEOID
Name: of census tract
below_povertyE: the estimated number of people below the poverty line
below_povertyM: the margin of error for below_povertyE
totalE: total estimated population
totalM: the margin of error for totalE
period: time period (either 2010 or 2017)



Show code
my_state <- "PA"
my_county <- "Philadelphia"

get_poverty <- function(yr) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    variables = c(below_poverty = "B07012_002", #this targets the people below the poverty line
                  total = "B07012_001"),
    state = my_state,
    county = my_county,
    year = yr,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide"
  ) |> 
    mutate(period = paste0(yr - 4, "_", yr))
}

# Fetch ACS data
poverty_change <- bind_rows(
  get_poverty(2010),
  get_poverty(2017)
) |> 
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"))

poverty_change$period <- substr(poverty_change$period, 6, nchar(poverty_change$period))

glimpse(poverty_change)

Part 2 — Test

2a. Computing the poverty rate

Poverty rate (share_) was calculated by dividing below_povertyE by totalE
Margin of error for poverty rate (share_moe) was calculated using the moe_prop() function in R



Show code
# compute poverty share & moe before creating wide dataframe
poverty_change <- poverty_change |> 
  mutate(
    share     = below_povertyE / totalE,
    share_moe = moe_prop(below_povertyE, totalE,
                         below_povertyM, totalM)
  )

# wrangling to wide format to MASTER DATAFRAME
poverty_master <- poverty_change |>
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, share, share_moe) |> 
  rename(moe = share_moe) |> 
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = c(share, moe)
  )

2b. Coefficient of variation
Coefficient of variation (cv) (in percentage) = (moe/1.645)/share * 100, where 1.645 is the z-score for a 90% two-tailed confidence level.


Show code
poverty_variation <- poverty_master |> 
  mutate(
    cv_2010 = (moe_2010 / 1.645)/share_2010 *100,
    cv_2017 = (moe_2017 / 1.645)/share_2017 *100,
  )

2c. Reliability table
A reliability table was built to show the poverty share, moe, and cv for each census tract and the associated reliability of the data based on the coefficient of variation.



Show code
reliability_table <- poverty_variation |> 
  mutate(
    dot_2010 = case_when(
      cv_2010 < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv_2010 <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE          ~ "🔴"
    ),
    dot_2017 = case_when(
      cv_2017 < 12  ~ "🟢",
      cv_2017 <= 40 ~ "🟡",
      TRUE          ~ "🔴"
    ),
    flag_2010 = case_when(
      cv_2010 < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv_2010 <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE          ~ "Unreliable"
    ),
    flag_2017 = case_when(
      cv_2017 < 12  ~ "Reliable",
      cv_2017 <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE          ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )


# Make it look nice using gt package
reliability_table |> 
  gt() |> 
  fmt_percent(columns = c(share_2010, share_2017), decimals = 1) |> 
  fmt_number(columns = c(moe_2010, moe_2017), decimals = 3) |> 
  fmt_number(columns = c(cv_2010, cv_2017), decimals = 1) |> 
  cols_label(
    dot_2010 = "",
    dot_2017 = "",
    NAME     = "County",
    share_2010 = "Poverty Share 2010",
    share_2017 = "Poverty Share 2017",
    moe_2010 = "MOE 2010",
    moe_2017 = "MOE 2017",
    cv_2010  = "CV 2010 (%)",
    cv_2017  = "CV 2017 (%)",
    flag_2010 = "Reliability 2010",
    flag_2017 = "Reliability 2017"
  ) |> 
  cols_move(
    columns = dot_2010,
    after = flag_2010
  ) |> 
  cols_move(
    columns = dot_2017,
    after = flag_2017
  ) |> 
  cols_align(align = "center", columns = c(dot_2010, dot_2017)) |> 
  tab_header(
    title    = "Population below 100% of the poverty level",
    subtitle = "Philadelphia tracts, ACS 5-year estimates"
  ) |> 
  tab_source_note(
    "Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable."
  )

2d. Computing poverty change, and associated margin of error
I will test whether the change is statistically distinguishable from zero at 90% confidence.
Reliability thresholds follow Jurjevich et al. (2018): CV < 12% reliable, 12–40% somewhat reliable, > 40% unreliable.
However, some troubleshooting is done first:


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_master |> 
  mutate(
    change   = `share_2017` - `share_2010`,
    se_2010  = `moe_2010` / 1.645,
    se_2017  = `moe_2017` / 1.645,
    se_diff  = sqrt(se_2010^2 + se_2017^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z        = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645    #using z-score for 90% confidence (2 tails)
  )

#Removing NA values
tested_NA <- poverty_tested |> 
  filter(change == "NaN")

head(tested_NA)


# A tibble: 6 × 13
  GEOID    NAME  share_2010 share_2017 moe_2010 moe_2017 change  se_2010 se_2017
  <chr>    <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
1 4210100… Cens…   NaN             NaN  NaN          NaN    NaN NaN          NaN
2 4210198… Cens…   NaN             NaN  NaN          NaN    NaN NaN          NaN
3 4210198… Cens…   NaN             NaN  NaN          NaN    NaN NaN          NaN
4 4210198… Cens…   NaN             NaN  NaN          NaN    NaN NaN          NaN
5 4210198… Cens…     0.0978        NaN    0.138      NaN    NaN   0.0837     NaN
6 4210198… Cens…   NaN             NaN  NaN          NaN    NaN NaN          NaN
# ℹ 4 more variables: se_diff <dbl>, moe_diff <dbl>, z <dbl>, significant <lgl>


Above: Detected NA values from dataframe
8 tracts displayed NA values for poverty shares for one/both surveys. To figure out what caused this, I input their GEOID into the census website to check their location. We can see that these tracts are located in non-residential areas. For example,

Tract 9804 covers the airport area
Tract 9806 covers the parking lot in Stadium
Tract 9808 covers Overbrooke Park

Therefore we will remove them from the dataset because it is irrelevant to poverty analysis of residents in Philadelphia.
For the remaining rows, we determine the number of significant changes:


Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_tested |> 
    filter(change != "NaN")

poverty_tested |> 
  count(significant)


# A tibble: 2 × 2
  significant     n
  <lgl>       <int>
1 FALSE         313
2 TRUE           63


Above: Count of tracts with a statistically significant change in poverty rate from 2010 to 2017
Only 63 out of 376 total tracts show a statistically detectable change across the 2 ACS surveys, which could mean that the article’s claims are not very valid.


2e. Visualising the change in poverty rates: A bar chart of the 15 most reliable tracts


Show code
poverty_tested |> 
  arrange(desc(moe_diff)) |> 
  slice_tail(n = 15) |>                                        # Of the 15 values with LOWEST moe
  mutate(NAME = str_remove(NAME, "Census Tract "),
         change = change * 100,
         moe_diff = moe_diff * 100) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, change), y = change)) +
  geom_col(fill = "forestgreen") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = change - moe_diff, ymax = change + moe_diff), width = 0.3) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in poverty rate (%) from 2006-2010 to 2013-2017",
    subtitle = "ACS 2023 5-year estimates, for the top 15 most statistically reliable tracts
    (based on lowest MoE)",
    x = "Census Tract number",
    y = "Change in poverty rate (%)"
  )









Above: Bar chart (with error bars) of poverty change in top 15 most reliable tracts
The margins of error (displayed in the error bars) are very large because it is the sum of the margins of error for both surveys.




Part 3 — Adjudicate
We will compute the article’s city-wide and neighbourhood-specific claims to check its accuracy. We will also test its statistical significance of the result we computed.

3a. Supported






NoteClaim 1



“Philadelphia has a 26% poverty rate from 2013-2017.”




Show code
# Calculate overall mean, moe, cv
poverty_tested |> 
  summarise(
    number_of_tracts   = n(),
    mean_share = mean(share_2017),
    mean_moe   = (moe_sum(moe = moe_2017, estimate = share_2017) / n()) ,
    mean_cv = (mean_moe / 1.645)/mean_share
  )


# A tibble: 1 × 4
  number_of_tracts mean_share mean_moe mean_cv
             <int>      <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>
1              376      0.260  0.00745  0.0174


The mean poverty rate across all tracts is indeed 26%, with a low coefficient of variation (cv) of 1.74%, indicating high reliability.


3b. Not supported






NoteClaim 2



“The neighborhood of Eastwick in Southwest Philadelphia, near Philadelphia International Airport, showed the greatest poverty-rate increase of any community, rocketing from 12 percent during 2006-10 to 26 percent in the newest survey. That means that even after the recession ended, around a decade ago, conditions in Eastwick have gotten much worse than during the depth of the downturn.”


Using the Census Geocoder, the approximate tract of Eastwick is Census Tract 61


Show code
# Calculate overall mean, moe, cv
poverty_tested |> 
  filter(NAME == "Census Tract 61") |> 
  select(GEOID, NAME, share_2017, share_2010, change, moe_diff, significant) |> 
  mutate(cv = (moe_diff / 1.645)/change) 


# A tibble: 1 × 8
  GEOID       NAME       share_2017 share_2010 change moe_diff significant    cv
  <chr>       <chr>           <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>       <dbl>
1 42101006100 Census Tr…      0.246      0.133  0.113    0.143 FALSE       0.765


Figures quoted are comparable enough, increasing from 13% during 2006-10 to 25% in the newest survey. However, the coefficient of variation is 76% which is very high, suggesting that there is no statistically detectable change from 2010 to 2017.


3c. Cannot be determined






NoteClaim 3



“Fairhill in North Philadelphia registered a stunning 61 percent poverty rate.”


Fairhill: Census Tract 176.02.


Show code
# Calculate overall mean, moe, cv
poverty_tested |> 
  filter(NAME == "Census Tract 176.02") |> 
  select(GEOID, NAME, share_2017, moe_2017) |> 
  mutate(cv = (moe_2017 / 1.645)/share_2017)


# A tibble: 1 × 5
  GEOID       NAME                share_2017 moe_2017    cv
  <chr>       <chr>                    <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl>
1 42101017602 Census Tract 176.02      0.614    0.122 0.121


Based on Jurjevich et al. (2018), the calculated poverty rate for Fairhill is accurate (61%), but only somewhat reliable based on the coefficient of variation of 12%. We will need to do more testing based on the surrounding tracts to create a more accurate profile of Fairhill.






NoteClaim 4



“White poverty throughout much of the city skyrocketed, led by the Northeast neighborhood of Holmesburg, which went from a 2 percent poverty rate to 19 percent.”


Holmesburg: Census Tract 326


Show code
# Calculate overall mean, moe, cv
poverty_tested |> 
  filter(NAME %in% c("Census Tract 326", "Census Tract 315.01")) |> 
  select(GEOID, NAME, share_2017, share_2010, change, moe_diff, z, significant) |> 
  mutate(cv = ((moe_diff / 1.645) / change) * 100) |> 
  select(NAME, share_2017, share_2010, change, significant, cv)


# A tibble: 2 × 6
  NAME                share_2017 share_2010 change significant    cv
  <chr>                    <dbl>      <dbl>  <dbl> <lgl>       <dbl>
1 Census Tract 315.01      0.166     0.0730 0.0928 FALSE        63.1
2 Census Tract 326         0.225     0.167  0.0574 FALSE       125. 



As seen from the results, equating Holmesburg to Tract 326 yielded very different values with a poverty rate of 17% in 2010, unlike the 2% rate that the article claimed.
Exploration of values in adjacent tracts showed high variability within Holmesburg - for example, the adjacent Tract 315.01 has a vastly different poverty rate of 7% in 2010.
While it is true that poverty rates “skyrocketed” to 17% and 22% across the two tracts, the significance is false. The article’s statement is not only statistically invalid, but also does not account for high variability within Holmesburg. The surrounding census tracts should be investigated as well.
Furthermore, the term “white poverty” will need to be verified by investigating the ethnic makeup of Holmesburg, to truly verify whether it is a mainly white population that is undergoing skyrocketing poverty.





Part 4 — Rewrite
Philadelphia’s poverty rate was ~26% in the 2013–2017 ACS, but neighbourhood-level comparisons are less straightforward than the original article suggests.

Fairhill’s estimated poverty rate was 61%, although further analysis of surrounding census tracts is needed to determine how well this figure represents the wider neighbourhood.
Eastwick’s poverty rate increased from about 13% in 2006–2010 to 25% in 2013–2017, but the large uncertainty around this change means that it is not statistically detectable.
Similarly, poverty increased substantially across the census tracts examined in Holmesburg, but the data does not establish that the change was statistically significant, nor that it was concentrated among white residents.

These results show substantial poverty across Philadelphia, while also highlighting the importance of accounting for uncertainty and variation between census tracts when interpreting neighbourhood-level changes.

Quarto is a publishing system mixing writing and code directly into a nice final document. 1. Writing in Markdown 2. Embedded R Code (+ tables, plots, results) in chunks 3. Quarto can render the document as a webpage (without needing any HTML code!), PDF, slide deck, or Word file.
Three places a file can live: 1. My computer - where I edit 2. GitHub.com - where it’s stored 3. My live site - what the world sees
Types of files and folders:

For me - index.qmd, about.qmd, weekly_notes.qmd, assignments.qmd
For the machine - quarto.yml (settings for whole website), _freeze (for quarto memory, after it gets rendered), .Rproj (for RStudio), .gitignore (for github), Renviron (for R, to keep secrets), docs/ (The Internet)

The loop: Edit → Save → Render → Commit → Push → wait → refresh

title: About Me!
text:
I just graduated from University College London in BSc Urban Studies, where I was first introduced to the world of spatial analysis. A year ago, I built my first map in QGIS, layering London’s air pollution over its social housing. What began as an experiment in technical flair turned into a moment of reckoning. The darkest reds traced the city’s most deprived neighborhoods, exposing inequality in color. That map taught me that data can clarify or conceal truth, reinforcing my beief that evidence-based approaches are foundational in making equitable and transparent policy decisions.
At Penn, I’m hoping to deepen my skills in geospatial analysis, machine learning, and data integration, while learning how to translate these insights into actionable strategies for policymakers and communities alike.

In this analysis, I look at median home value across counties in New Jersey, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably. I just moved to the US, and was picked up by my uncle who lives in NJ - I would love to know more about the beautiful houses there and how property prices compare!

section: How big is the margin of error?

How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

section: Optimising categories of margin of error
text:
Optimising categories of margin of error
To comput categories for margins of error, Jenks breaks are used to minimise variance within each of the 3 categories of confidence.

library(classInt)

jenks <- classInt::classIntervals(
  county_data$moe_pct,
  n = 3,
  style = "jenks"
)

jenks$brks

[1] 0.8147052 1.3736873 1.8632479 2.9757848

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
Sorting counties into reliability categories

county_data <- county_data |> 
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct <= jenks$brks[2] ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct <= jenks$brks[3] ~ "Moderate confidence",
    TRUE                    ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

county_wide <- county_wide |> 
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) |> 
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct <= jenks$brks[2]  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct <= jenks$brks[3] ~ "Moderate confidence",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now we compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide |> 
  group_by(reliability) |> 
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  ) |>

There doesn’t seem to be a trend between confidence and population size. Maybe the categories of confidence are too arbitrary.
It would be better to plot, using the actual numerical values of margins of error!

Scatterplot of margins of error against population size

# Generate scatterplot
ggplot(
  data = county_wide,
  mapping = aes(x = popE, y = moe_pct)
) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm")








We see a downwards trends based on the best-fit line.

# Computing Pearson's correlation coefficient
cor(county_wide$popE, county_wide$moe_pct, use = "complete.obs")

[1] -0.6136624


The Pearson’s correlation coefficient indicates that there is a moderately strong negative correlation between population and margin of error (-0.6136624), indicating that as population size increases, the margin of error for house values decreases. This corresponds to how a larger sample size increases reliability as it reduces random error.

5 34017 Hudson County…      508600       12318    2.42 Low confid… 508600 710478

The county we can most safely predict house values of is Middlesex County, with a median house value of $440,000. They have the lowest margin of error of 0.81%, thanks to its relatively high population of 860,000.
We have the lowest confidence regarding median home values in Salem County, with the lowest population of 65,000 which likely contributes to its high margin of error of 2.98%.
That’s because the 5-year ACS only samples approximately 5% of households over 5 years in total, rather than a complete count of all housing units. A smaller county would yield a smaller sample size, increasing random error for house value estimates. The use of the median value, however, helps to counter the effect of random error by ignoring extremes.
What could go wrong?
The margin of error introduces false positives about a place for policy analysis. If a county has a high estimated median house value, but also high margin of error, the state might incorrectly conclude that housing is more expensive in that area and allocate less housing assistance (and vice versa). This means resources are not allocated optimally to those in need. This is particularly disadvantageous for those who live in smaller counties with high margins of error whose needs are not represented in the census well.

title: Week 2: dplyr and The Census
text:
The Census

First started a decennial census - every 10 years, each person is asked 10 questions
Then formalised into an American Community Survey (ACS) –> samples 3% of households to generate a population estimate

1-year ACS: Places > 65,000 (not very useful)
5-year ACS: Per tract; average over 5 years of samples (e.g. 2011-2015 to generate 2016 census) –> Dead now :()
Each Base Table has a table number (19013) + line number (001 - means base row, total households) + margin of error - MoE (E) e.g. B19013_001E
Scales - State –> County –> Tract (Neighborhood, 5000-8000 people; boundaries always change) –> Block groups (but high MoE) –> Block (Decennial only)

Longitudinal tracts have been made (NHGIS/LTDB)




Calling data from tidycensus

library(tidycensus)
load_variables()
GEOID - a unique identifier


First 2 digits: state
Next 3 digits: county
Next 6 digits: tract
+1 extra number


To look at codes: vars <- load_variables(2023, “acs5”)
